newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Gaza conference shows PLO weakness.
newsitem.headline: Gaza conference shows PLO weakness.

text.p: With bulldozers about to complete the wall of Jewish housing cutting off Arab East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank, Yasser Arafat is pressing every political panic button he can reach.

The Palestinian president has been to the White House, the United Nations in New York, and Arab capitals attempting to keep the international spotlight on Israel's controversial plan to replace pine trees with concrete on a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
The politicking culminated on Saturday in a meeting of Western, Arab and Asian countries that the PLO leader organized as an "international conference" to save Middle East peace.
Arafat declared his meeting with the local diplomatic representatives of the United States, the European Union, Russia, Japan, Egypt and Jordan, had helped save peace talks.
But Western and Palestinian analysts said the conference highlighted the weakness of Arafat's position against the centre-right government of Benjamin Netanyahu in the battle for Jerusalem.
"It does reflect the weakness of the Palestinians," said Ghassan al-Khatib, a former peace negotiator and analyst.
He said Palestinian officials had tried to build up what was little more than a routine briefing for diplomats into an international gathering.
"He can't do much to prevent Netanyahu from building," said political analyst and writer Ali Jirbawi. "But he is trying to get internal support among Palestinians and outside support."

"Since the peace process began in Madrid the Palestinians have been working on symbols as much as facts on the ground...This is a message to people that he is a leader who can ask the world to come and they come, despite Israel," Jirbawi said.

Jerusalem is a powerful symbol and reality for both sides in the century-old Jewish-Palestinian conflict. Both Arafat and Netanyahu want to parlay a strong presence on the ground into leverage at the negotiating table. Talks on the final status of Jerusalem are scheduled to resume this month and be completed within two years.
Analysts said Arafat's diplomatic shuttling and Gaza meeting are also an attempt by the PLO chairman to shield himself from finger-pointing if political protest spills into the street.

Last time Netanyahu made a move in East Jerusalem -- opening a second entrance to a tunnel near holy places -- Palestinian youths stoned Israeli troops. When the Israelis opened fire Arafat's armed police responded. The unprecedented gunbattles killed 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers.
"He is trying to get off the hook of any responsibility for any future developments," said Khatib.
"Arafat has tried the international arena and is not getting much of a positive response," he added.

PLO officials say they expect protests if Netanyahu starts breaking ground for the settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim, Har Homa in Hebrew, early next week. But they insist the protests will remain peaceful.
Israel has warned the Palestinians against violence and drawn up contingency plans to deal with unrest.
The U.S. consul-general in Jerusalem, Edward Abington, said last week Arafat had assured him he did not want violence, noting the September fighting had hurt the Palestinians.
"I take at face value what the Chairman has said that he doesn't want violence," Abington said.
Analysts said Arafat was trying to balance keeping the United States happy by continuing peace talks with showing his people that he championed their rights.
"He is leaving himself room for manoeuvre," said Jirbawi. "He cannot come out and call upon people to prevent the settlement building."
Khatib wonders whether ordinary Palestinians would heed such a call in any case, given that the fighting in September did not lead to the closing of the tunnel.

"People need a leadership they trust in terms of translating their sacrifice into a strong political position and achievements, he said. "Relations and the level of trust between the public and the Palestinain Authority is not so high...so the level of response is low."
Palestinian analysts and Israeli security sources said they expected the scale of demonstrations against the settlement to pick up, especially if protesters had bulldozers as a spark.
Several said this time the fire would be harder to light but also harder to put out.
As for Arafat, he left the world guessing. Asked after the Gaza meeting if he expected violence next week he said: "I don't know. Ask the Palestinian masses."
